entities.summary:
The avant-garde movement emerged in the early 20th century as a radical challenge to traditional art forms and literary conventions. This group of artists, writers, and musicians sought to revolutionize the way people experienced and interpreted art, often incorporating experimental techniques and pushing the boundaries of what was considered acceptable. The avant-garde's influence can be seen in the development of modern and contemporary art, as well as in the rise of new literary movements such as Surrealism and Dadaism.

The avant-garde's impact on modern society was significant, as it helped to create a new cultural landscape that valued innovation and experimentation over traditional forms of art. This movement also played a key role in shaping the development of modern film, with many avant-garde filmmakers going on to become influential directors in their own right.

One of the most famous avant-garde artists was Marcel Duchamp, who is widely regarded as one of the most influential artists of the 20th century. Duchamp's work, including his famous 'readymades' such as 'Fountain' and 'L.H.O.O.Q.', challenged traditional notions of what constitutes art and paved the way for future generations of artists.

The avant-garde's legacy can also be seen in the many festivals and events that celebrate its innovations, such as the Venice Biennale and the Documenta art festivals. These events bring together artists and art lovers from around the world to celebrate the avant-garde's continued influence on contemporary art and culture.

In conclusion, the avant-garde movement was a pivotal moment in the history of art and literature, marking a significant turning point in the development of modern culture. Its influence can still be seen today, and its legacy continues to shape the way we experience and interpret art and literature.
